title: Valmiki and Narada
hook: a poet named after an anthill and a sage who never stays in one place
tomorrow: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Valmiki and Narada, and the short Ramayana, the whole story told in chapter one. Did someone enjoy hearing a story they already knew? Today, the two men themselves. Day four hundred ninety-two.

Valmika is a Sanskrit word for an anthill, the tall mound of earth termites and ants build. And the poet who gave the world the Ramayana is called Valmiki: the one from the anthill. Why would anyone be named that? There's a story people tell about it, and it's one of the best-known stories of a changed life in India. But here's the honest part. Valmiki's own Ramayana doesn't tell it. In his own book he is simply a hermit, living by a river, asking a good question.
screen: `VALMIKA: AN ANTHILL.` → `THE ONE FROM THE ANTHILL.` → `A STORY HIS OWN BOOK DOESN'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Start with Narada. He's a devarshi, a sage of the gods, and he's everywhere in Hindu storytelling: the Mahabharata, the Puranas, folk plays. He wanders between heaven and earth, carries news, asks the question that sets things moving, and in later tradition he walks with a vina, singing the name of Vishnu. In the Ramayana he arrives, answers Valmiki, and leaves. A visitor who changes everything and doesn't stay. Now Valmiki. Later texts and countless retellings say he began life as a highway robber, often called Ratnakara, who robbed travelers to feed his family. One day he stopped a group of sages, sometimes Narada himself. They asked: will your family share the weight of your wrongdoing? He went home and asked. They said no. Shaken, he asked the sages for help, and was given the name of Rama to repeat. He couldn't even say it properly, so he said mara, mara, which run together becomes Rama, Rama. He sat so long that an anthill rose over him. That's a story people tell, and many people love it. It's found in later works, not in Valmiki's Sanskrit text. In his own Ramayana, Valmiki is a muni, a quiet sage. And in the epic's last book, he steps into the story: Sita will find shelter in his hermitage. Today, many people, especially the Valmiki community of North India, honor him as their own guru, and his birthday is celebrated each autumn.
screen: `NARADA: THE SAGE WHO WANDERS.` · `THE ROBBER STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `MARA, MARA BECOMES RAMA, RAMA.` · `IN HIS OWN BOOK, A QUIET SAGE.` · then, large: `VĀLMĪKI, THE ONE FROM THE ANTHILL.`

segments.voice: Sit very still, the way the story says Valmiki sat. Imagine the earth slowly rising around you, grain by grain, while you stay. Not heavy. Just held. Let your breath be the only thing that moves. If you pray, you can repeat a name that's sacred to you, softly, and if the words get jumbled, let them. The bell holds the time.
Valmiki and Narada. The hermit-poet whose name means the one from the anthill, and the wandering sage of the gods who answers his question.
Your line: Valmiki and Narada. Today, think of someone whose life took a turn nobody expected, maybe yours, and give the later chapters as much weight as the early ones. Day four hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Valmiki Jayanti, his birthday, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Ashvin, especially by the Valmiki community, who honor him as their guru; Narada appears across Hindu scripture and is remembered as a great devotee of Vishnu.

original.note: Sanskrit valmīka: an anthill. Vālmīki, the one from the anthill.

trapdoor: what you thought: Valmiki was a robber, and his book says so.
what it means: the robber story is a beloved later telling; in his own text he is a quiet sage.

what a scholar hears: the Ratnakara story and the mara-mara chant appear in later texts such as the Adhyatma Ramayana and regional retellings; Valmiki's Bala Kanda calls him simply a muni and tapasvi.

notes: Sources for the Ratnakara story: commonly traced to the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Bengali Krittivasi Ramayana, among others; confirm the citations. Details (the family's answer, mara-mara) vary by telling.
The Valmiki community (Balmiki) and Valmiki Jayanti (Ashvin purnima) are mentioned respectfully; a Keeper should confirm the wording is welcome.
Narada's vina and Vishnu devotion are later tradition, described as such.

Sita in Valmiki's hermitage comes from the Uttara Kanda, which many scholars regard as a later addition; the teach now says 'in the epic's last book' rather than presenting it as uncontested. 'Conversion story' changed to 'a changed life' to avoid a religious-conversion reading.
